Direct-acting electric radiators (often called electric resistance heaters) are very efficient at the point of use, but their overall “energy efficiency” depends on how you measure it:

1. Point-of-use efficiency  
   • Electric resistance heating converts virtually 100 % of the incoming electrical energy into heat in the room.  
   • There are no boiler losses or distribution‐pipe losses as with water-based systems.

2. Primary-energy and cost considerations  
   • Electricity generation and transmission typically incur losses (depending on the grid mix, losses from power plants and transmission can be 30–40 %).  
   • As a result, if you judge efficiency on a primary-energy basis (i.e. including production and delivery), direct electric heating is less efficient than heat‐pump systems or district heating.  
   • Electricity is often more expensive per kWh than district heat or gas, so running costs tend to be higher.

Below are several measures—ranging from simple to more advanced—that can be adopted in residential buildings:

An energy declaration (in Swedish: energideklaration) is an official document—often called an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC)—that describes a building’s energy use, energy performance and suggestions for improvement. In Sweden it is required by law when you construct a new building, when you sell or let an existing building, or when you undertake a major renovation.

• Building description – type of building, heated floor area (Atemp), number of floors and stairwells, construction materials, etc.  
• Measured or calculated energy use – usually expressed in kWh per square meter and year, and converted into a standardized energy performance class (A through G, where A is best).  
• Primary energy factors – showing total energy demand including production and distribution losses.

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any measure or upgrade that reduces a building’s energy demand, lowers its energy bills and cuts its carbon emissions. In practice, it means making the building fabric, installations and systems perform more efficiently so that you need less fuel or electricity to maintain comfort and functionality.  

Typical energy-efficiency improvements include  
• Thermal insulation upgrades (walls, roof, floor)  
• High-performance windows and doors (e.g. triple-glazed units)  
• Heat-recovery ventilation or improved airtightness to reduce losses  
• Modern, efficient heating and cooling systems (e.g. condensing boilers, heat pumps)  
• LED lighting and smart controls  
• Building-integrated renewables (e.g. solar panels)

In most buildings, the largest electricity end-uses typically fall into the following categories:

1. Space heating (when served by electric heat pumps or direct-electric heaters)  
2. Domestic hot water preparation (electric water heaters or heat-pump water heaters)  
3. Household appliances and consumer electronics (refrigerators, washing machines, TVs, computers, etc.)  
4. Lighting (fixed interior and exterior luminaires)  
5. Mechanical systems – ventilation fans, circulation pumps and, where present, air-conditioning compressors  
6. Miscellaneous loads (elevators, kitchen equipment, charging of electric vehicles, specialized process or office equipment)

Roughly speaking, in a modern electrically heated home the heat pump or electric heater may account for 40–60 % of total electricity use, hot water 10–20 %, appliances and electronics 20–30 %, lighting 5–15 %, and ventilation/pumps a further 5–10 %. Natural (passive) ventilation—using window openings, vents or architectural features to drive air movement—offers several advantages over fully mechanical systems.  Below are the main benefits:

1. Lower energy consumption and operating cost  
   • No fans or blowers are required, so electricity use is minimized.  
   • Reduced running costs compared to mechanical ventilation or air‐handling units.  

2. Simpler installation and maintenance  
   • Fewer moving parts and no ducted fans means less complexity.  
   • Lower capital cost for equipment and simpler annual checks.  

3. Improved indoor air quality perception and comfort  
   • Direct connection to the outdoor environment can enhance occupants’ sense of freshness.  
   • Variable airflow rates under occupants’ control (e.g. opening windows) can improve satisfaction.

Optimizing natural ventilation in a house is a matter of combining good architectural design, careful placement of openings and simple passive-ventilation strategies. Below are the key principles and practical measures:

1. Orientation and Floor-Plan Layout  
   • Align main living spaces and bedroom zones along the prevailing wind direction to maximize cross-ventilation.  
   • Create clear through-flows by placing windows or vents on opposite walls or ends of a room or corridor.  
   • Use an open-plan layout or internal glazed screens rather than solid partitions so that air can move freely between rooms.

2. Window and Opening Design  
   • Size and position: Provide both low-level inlets (e.g. windows or vents near the floor) to admit cool air, and high-level outlets (e.g. clerestory windows, roof-lights, or louvres) to exhaust warm air.  
   • Operability: Install windows with easy-to-adjust restrictors or friction hinges that allow precise control over opening width and airflow

Electricity bills in Sweden (and in many other countries) are made up of several components, and your total consumption (kWh) enters into most of them. Here’s how your usage affects what you pay:

1. Fixed fee (subscription)  
   – This is a set monthly or annual charge from your electricity supplier and your network company. It does not depend on how much you use, but covers administrative costs and the right to be connected.

2. Variable energy charge (price per kWh)  
   – This is the part that directly scales with your consumption. If you use twice as many kilowatt-hours, you pay twice as much in energy charges.  
   – In a simple “fixed-price” contract, the supplier’s price per kWh is the same regardless of how much you consume.  
   – In a “block tariff” contract, the price per kWh can increase once you pass certain annual or monthly consumption thresholds (for example, the first 5 000 kWh at one rate, the next 5 000 kWh at a higher rate).

Control and regulation technology (often called “styr- och reglerteknik” in Swedish) is the discipline—and the associated hardware and software—used to maintain and optimize the performance of building installations (heating, ventilation, air-conditioning, lighting, etc.). Its main purpose is to keep environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, air quality, brightness) at desired set-points while minimizing energy use and ensuring safety.  

Key elements  
1. Sensors – measure physical quantities (e.g. temperature, CO₂ levels, flow, pressure, light).  
2. Actuators – execute adjustments (e.g. valves, dampers, variable-speed drives on pumps or fans).  
3. Controllers – process sensor data and compute control actions, using methods such as on/off, PID or more advanced model-based algorithms.  
4. Communication/networking – links sensors, actuators and controllers in a building automation or BMS (Building Management System).  
5. User interfaces and software – allow facility managers

In the electric‐vehicle sector there isn’t a single globally mandated cut-off, but a practical industry convention is as follows:

• “Normal” (or “slow”) AC charging  
  – Typically up to 7 kW at home  
  – Often extended to about 11–22 kW at destination chargers (e.g. workplace, public parking)  

• “Fast” (or DC) charging  
  – Generally starts at around 50 kW DC  
  – Delivers higher power (often 50–150 kW) to refill batteries much more quickly  

Some operators further subdivide “fast” into:  
  – Fast DC charging: 50–150 kW  
  – Ultra-fast (or “rapid”) charging: >150 kW  

In short, if you’re charging with AC up to ~22 kW it’s considered normal; once you move to dedicated DC stations delivering 50 kW or more, you’ve entered the fast-charging regime.

In Sweden (and per most European lighting standards), the generally recommended maintained illuminance in stairwells is as follows:

• 100 lx (lux) on the walking surface (horizontal plane) for normal everyday use.  
• A minimum uniformity (U₁) of around 0.4 – 0.6 (that is, Eₘᵢₙ/Eₐᵥₑ ≥ 0.4) to avoid strong light‐dark contrasts on steps.  

In addition, for emergency/escape‐route lighting your design should ensure:  
• At least 1 lx on the floor level along the escape path when mains power fails.  
• A uniformity ratio (U₁) of at least 0.1 in emergency operation.

These levels help ensure safe, comfortable visibility in both normal and emergency situations.

In Sweden, common parts of residential buildings – including stairwells – are normally design­ed to be kept at a minimum indoor temperature of 16 °C (measured at 1 m above the floor, 0.5 m from the exterior wall). In practice most housing companies set stairwell heaters so that the steady-state temperature reaches about 18 °C, which

• prevents cold-weather condensation and frost damage in building elements  
• ensures a safe, draught-free environment for residents  
• complies with Boverket’s Building Regulations (BBR)  

If you have a more stringent local regulation or a special use-case (e.g. high visitor traffic, accessibility for the elderly), you may choose to set the temperature closer to 18–20 °C. Always verify against your municipality’s building code or your building’s energy performance certificate for any specific requirements.

Ventilation balancing is the process of commissioning a building’s mechanical ventilation system so that the actual airflows in each supply- and exhaust-air terminal match the values specified in the design. In practice this means adjusting fan speeds, dampers or valves, and sometimes ductwork, until each room or zone receives the correct amount of fresh air and exhaust air.
